> Part of [**RentSignal**](https://rentsignal.de) — an AI rent-optimization engine for the German rental market.

Here is a result that should bother you: in Berlin rental data, apartments *with* a balcony rent for slightly **less** per square meter than apartments without one. Taken at face value, that says a landlord should rip the balcony off to charge more. Obviously wrong. So what's going on — and what does a balcony *actually* add to the rent?

This is a textbook confounding problem, and it has a clean causal answer. The trick is controlling for the right things — including some confounders that didn't used to be measurable at all.

## Why the naive number lies

Balconies don't appear at random. They cluster in particular kinds of buildings — and in Berlin, that correlation runs the "wrong" way for a naive comparison. Many balconies sit on older *Altbau* stock that is less renovated, darker, or in a less central location. The apartment rents for less not *because* of the balcony but because of everything the balcony travels with. The balcony takes the blame for its company.

Formally, we want the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) — how much more an apartment rents *because* it has feature $T$, holding the confounders $X$ fixed:

$$
\text{ATT} = \mathbb{E}\big[\,Y(1) - Y(0)\,\big|\, T = 1\,\big].
$$

The naive difference in means estimates this only if treatment is independent of the potential outcomes given nothing — which it plainly isn't. We need to condition on $X$.

## The data and the design

I worked from **~4,800 regular Berlin listings** scraped in 2026. The first important decision was what to *exclude*: **41.5%** of the raw listings were *Tauschwohnungen* — apartment swaps offered at deliberately below-market rent (median €10.37/m² versus €19.00/m² for regular listings). Their price is set by rent control and swap dynamics, not by amenities, so leaving them in would poison every treatment-effect estimate. Out they went.

Then **propensity-score matching**: for each treated apartment, find an untreated apartment that looks just like it on the confounders, compare their rents, average the gaps. The estimate is only as good as the confounder set — and this is where it gets interesting. The model controls for **27 confounders**, including three categories that a hedonic regression from a decade ago simply couldn't see:

- **Structural** — size, rooms, building era, floor, condition.
- **Spatial** — distance to the centre, U-Bahn, parks and water; food/café/shop counts within 500–1000 m; and satellite vegetation/water/built-up indices (NDVI / NDWI / NDBI) from Sentinel-2.
- **Visual, from AI** — `renovation_level`, `interior_quality`, `brightness`, and `building_condition`, extracted from listing photos by a Gemini vision model.

That last group is the key to the paradox. A balcony correlates with older, less-renovated buildings — so unless you can *measure* renovation and interior quality, you can't separate the balcony's effect from the building's. AI-extracted image features finally let you hold "how nice and renovated does this place look" constant while you vary the balcony.

## The paradox, resolved

With the full confounder set, balance is excellent (30/30 covariates with standardized mean difference < 0.1 on the matched balcony sample) and the balcony's effect **flips sign**:

| Feature | v1 (2019 data, 11 confounders) | v2 (2026 data, 27 confounders + AI vision) |
|---|---|---|
| **Balcony** | **−€0.72 / m²** | **+€1.08 / m²**  `[0.21, 1.97]` |
| Kitchen | +€2.91 | **+€3.48 / m²**  `[2.81, 4.20]` |
| Elevator | +€1.09 | **+€1.59 / m²**  `[0.75, 2.48]` |
| Garden | +€0.93 | **+€1.36 / m²**  `[0.53, 2.17]` |

The first version of this analysis — older data, no image or spatial controls — reproduced the paradox: a *negative* balcony effect. Adding the renovation and interior-quality confounders does exactly what the theory says it should. Once you stop letting "old and shabby" hide inside "has a balcony," the balcony's true premium emerges: **about +€1.08/m²**, with a 95% confidence interval comfortably above zero. For a 75 m² apartment that's roughly **+€80/month** that the naive number was throwing away.

Kitchen comes out as the dominant fitted feature at **+€3.48/m²**, and its premium is heterogeneous across building eras — strongest in older and mid-century stock, near zero in post-2015 new-builds where a modern kitchen is simply expected.

## New premiums you couldn't measure before

Because the confounders come from photos, the *treatments* can too. Beyond the classic four, I estimated effects for features that only a vision model can reliably tag across thousands of listings:

| Feature (AI-detected) | Causal effect | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| **High ceilings** | **+€1.97 / m²** | `[0.59, 3.28]` |
| **Dielen (plank) floors** | **+€1.28 / m²** | `[0.17, 2.33]` |
| Cellar | −€0.90 / m² | `[−1.56, −0.22]` |

High ceilings and original plank floors — the hallmarks of desirable Berlin *Altbau* — carry real, identifiable premiums once you can detect them at scale. (The cellar's negative sign is almost certainly residual confounding with older peripheral buildings, a useful reminder that not every coefficient is a clean causal effect.) As far as I can tell, using AI-extracted image features as *treatment indicators* in a hedonic matching design is novel — the photos become both the controls and the variables of interest.

## Why this matters

Two takeaways, one methodological and one practical.

**Methodologically:** the balcony paradox is a clean, visceral demonstration that *better confounders change conclusions* — not by a little, but by flipping a sign. Multimodal data (satellite + vision) isn't a gimmick here; it's what makes the un-confounding actually possible. The missing variable was "how renovated is this apartment," and for the first time it's measurable.

**Practically:** for a rent-optimization product, the difference between "balconies cost you money" and "a balcony adds ~€80/month" is the difference between bad advice and good advice. Causal estimates — not raw correlations or even SHAP feature importances — are what you want when the output is a recommendation someone will act on.

The naive number wasn't wrong because the data was bad. It was wrong because a balcony rarely travels alone.
